migrationNotes: Spine: a crowd wandering at random between two rooms, then the same crowd as dissolved particles on either side of a membrane.
Each screen adds one condition: random wandering makes a net drift, equal sizes give an equal share, a balance keeps both flows going, and the membrane decides whether anything crosses.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-diffusion-and-membranes-diff-check, -total-why, -perm-check. Their meaning is covered by other items.

lesson.title: Which way will molecules move?

steps.headline: Two rooms and an open door

lead.text: Look at the rooms a little more closely. Everyone wanders at random, but the doorway is the same for everybody, so the number who cross in each direction depends only on how many people are in each room. Suppose that in each minute a quarter of the people in a room happen to go through the door.

In the first minute a quarter of the 20 people on the left (5 people) cross to the right, while a quarter of the 4 people on the right (1 person) crosses to the left. Five go one way and one goes the other, so the difference between the two crossings is 4 people. That difference is the net movement: 4 people from left to right. The rooms now hold 16 and 8.

The second minute works the same way. A quarter of 16 is 4 and a quarter of 8 is 2, so the net movement falls to 2 people and the rooms hold 14 and 10. Each minute the net movement is half what it was, because the gap between the rooms is half what it was.

afterFigure.text: Nobody pushes the crowd out of the full room. It drifts because a crowded room has more people to send through the door than a sparse one, and the closer the rooms get to equal numbers, the slower the drift becomes. The same counting works for anything that moves at random, which includes the particles in a cell.

diagram.alt: Two rooms of equal size joined by a doorway, with dots for people. At the start the left room has 20 people and the right room 4. After the first minute 5 have crossed to the right and 1 to the left, leaving 16 and 8. After the second minute 4 and 2 have crossed, leaving 14 and 10.
diagram.caption: A quarter of each room goes through the door every minute. Use the buttons to step through the minutes and compare the two crossings.

lead.text: Back to the rooms as they began, with a crowd wandering at random through an open door.

Now swap the people for particles. When sugar or a dye dissolves in water it breaks up into separate particles. The dissolved substance is called a solute. Water molecules are always jostling the solute particles, so each one wanders at random, just like a person in the rooms.

Replace the rooms with two compartments of equal size and the doorway with a membrane that lets the solute through, and the same counting applies. The word for how crowded a solute is in a given space is its concentration. Because the compartments are the same size, the side with more particles is the side with the higher concentration.

afterFigure.text: Move the slider under the picture. The particles drift towards equal numbers on the two sides, and the movement slows as they level out. This net movement of a substance from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated is called diffusion. Either side can be the more concentrated one, so the direction comes from comparing the two.
With the direction settled, the next thing to find out is how far the movement goes before it stops.

lead.text: Apply the rule to a new pair of compartments, equal in size.

The net movement stops when the two sides are equally concentrated. With compartments of the same size, that happens when they hold the same amount, and a state where the net movement has stopped is called equilibrium.

To find the equal amount, remember that diffusion only moves particles from one side to the other. None is made and none is lost, so the total on the two sides stays fixed. Add the two sides together, then split the total evenly.
Take 9 units on one side and 3 on the other. The total is 12, so at equilibrium each side holds 6. The crowded side falls from 9 to 6, so 3 units must cross.

afterFigure.text: Move the slider in each case. The second one also has a total of 12, so it settles at 6 on each side too, and this time the right side is the crowded one that loses units.

lead.text: Add the two sides, then share the total between the equal volumes.

Return to the two rooms once they hold 12 people each. A visitor looking in would see no change, because the counts stay put. The wandering has not stopped, though. A quarter of each room, which is 3 people, still goes through the door every minute, in each direction.

The traffic through the door is as busy as ever, but the two crossings are equal and cancel out. That is what equilibrium means: the net movement is zero while the people, or the particles, go on moving. In the compartments, individual particles keep crossing both ways at the same rate, and the amount on each side stays the same. In the picture the first case is at equilibrium and the second is not.

afterFigure.text: This matters to a living cell. A cell that keeps using up the oxygen reaching it holds less oxygen per unit of space than its surroundings, so the net movement never falls to zero. Oxygen keeps arriving through the membrane, and the cell spends no effort bringing it in.

lead.text: Two compartments of equal size have reached equilibrium, and solute is still crossing between them.

Everything so far assumed that the solute could cross. A real membrane has a say in that, as the doorkeeper from the first lesson does. A membrane is permeable to a substance if that substance can cross it, and impermeable to it if it cannot.
Those words describe a membrane's behaviour towards one substance at a time. The same membrane can be permeable to water and impermeable to a dye.

afterFigure.text: Compare the cases. When the dye can cross, the sides level out. When it cannot, each side keeps the amount it started with, no matter how different they are, because nothing crosses to change them. A difference in concentration produces movement only when the substance can get through.
So the first question to ask about any membrane is what can cross it. Water often can when a solute cannot, and the next lesson follows what happens then.

lead.text: Now take away every route across the barrier.

lesson.orientation: Predict net diffusion from concentration and membrane permeability.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A cell trades with the world around it all day. Food and oxygen come in and waste goes out, and every item has to cross the membrane we met in the last lesson. For much of this traffic the cell does no pushing at all, yet the goods still move in a steady direction.

The pattern is easiest to see at a bigger scale. Picture two rooms of equal size joined by an open doorway. At the start 20 people stand in the left room and 4 in the right. Everyone wanders about at random, and nobody has been told which way to go.

After a while the numbers in the two rooms will have changed, and the way they change follows a rule that particles in water obey as well. This lesson finds that rule, then puts a membrane in the doorway and sees what changes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict which way a dissolved substance moves across a membrane, and when it will not move at all.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains how cells take in nutrients without spending energy.

recap.keyIdea: A solute that can cross a membrane moves net from the crowded side to the sparse side until the concentrations match. A solute that cannot cross stays put.

blocks.text: You followed 24 people to equal numbers in two rooms, shared units of solute between equal compartments, and saw that a solute the membrane blocks keeps its starting amount. Back at the doorway, you can now say which way a crowd of particles drifts and when it stops.

recap.nextHook: A membrane can pass water and stop a solute, and the next lesson asks what happens to the water when it does.

questions.prompt: Equal volumes hold 12 solute units on the left and 4 on the right, and solute can cross. In which direction is there net movement at first?
hints: Which side is more concentrated? With equal volumes, compare the amounts.
Which side sends more particles across the membrane?
Net movement runs away from the crowded side.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left side is more concentrated, so net solute movement is to the right.

questions.onCorrect: Left to right: from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs from the sparser side to the crowded one. Net movement goes the other way.
The two sides differ in concentration, so more particles cross one way than the other.

questions.prompt: Two fixed equal volumes contain 10 and 6 units of freely crossing solute. How many units are on each side at equilibrium?
hints: Keep the total solute constant.
Add the amounts on the two sides.
Divide the total between two equal volumes.
questions.onCorrect: 8 each. Total solute stays constant, and equal volumes finish with equal amounts.

misconceptions.feedback: That's both sides together. Share it between the two compartments.
That's the left side's starting amount. Some of it has moved across.

questions.prompt: 12 solute units start on the left and 4 on the right. The barrier blocks both solute and water. How many solute units are on the left after a long time?
hints: Check what can cross first.
If nothing can cross, can any amount change?
Each side keeps the amount it started with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nothing can cross, so each side keeps its starting amount: 12 on the left.

questions.onCorrect: 12. A barrier that blocks the solute leaves the amounts unchanged, whatever the difference in concentration.

misconceptions.feedback: That would need solute to cross, and this barrier blocks it.
That's the right side's amount. Ask about the left side.

questions.prompt: At equal concentration, 8 units are on each side. How many solute units are in the whole two-compartment system?
hints: Count both compartments.
There are eight units in each.
Add the two equal amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 + 8 = 16 units. Diffusion does not destroy solute.

questions.onCorrect: 16. Equilibrium means equal concentrations, not missing solute: the total is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That's one side. Count both compartments.

questions.prompt: At diffusion equilibrium, which statement is accurate?
hints: Separate no net change from no motion.

acceptedIdeas: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equilibrium is dynamic: opposite flows balance on average.

choices.label: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
All molecules move in one direction

questions.onCorrect: Particles keep crossing both ways at equal rates, so there is no net flow.

misconceptions.feedback: Particles keep moving. What stops is the net change in concentration.
One-way movement would keep changing the concentrations. At equilibrium the flows balance.

questions.prompt: A separate equal-volume system starts with 14 solute units on one side and 2 on the other. How many units must move net from the concentrated side to reach equilibrium?
hints: Find the equilibrium amount first.
The total is shared between two equal volumes.
Subtract the equilibrium amount from the starting amount on the crowded side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each side finishes with 8. The concentrated side loses 14 − 8 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Find the equal share first, then see how far the crowded side must fall to reach it.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the amount each side ends with. How many had to move to get there?
That's the gap between the sides. Only half of the gap has to cross.

questions.prompt: A membrane is permeable to water but not to a dye. 9 dye units are on the left and 3 on the right. How many dye units are on the left after a long time?
hints: Which substances can cross this membrane?
Can the dye cross?
If the dye cannot move, its amounts stay as they began.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The dye cannot cross, so its amounts do not change: 9 on the left.

questions.onCorrect: 9. The dye cannot cross, so a concentration difference moves nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what each side would hold if the dye could cross. Check what the membrane lets through.
That's the right side's amount. Ask about the left.

questions.prompt: Two equal rooms are joined by an open door. 20 people start in the left room and 4 in the right, and everyone wanders at random. After a long time, how many people are in the left room?
hints: Does anyone leave the building, or arrive?
Count everyone in both rooms together.
Think about sharing that crowd between two equal rooms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Everyone is still in the building: 20 + 4 = 24. Equal rooms end up with equal crowds: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. People cross both ways, but more leave the crowded room, so the rooms settle at equal numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: That's where the left room started. People keep crossing the door, so the count changes.
That's everyone in the building. The question asks about the left room only.

questions.prompt: Dye is dropped into still water. Overall, where does the dye move?
hints: Which region sends more particles across the boundary between them?

acceptedIdeas: From where it is crowded to where it is not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net movement runs from the more concentrated region to the less concentrated one.

choices.label: From where it is crowded to where it is not
From where it is sparse to where it is crowded

questions.onCorrect: From crowded to sparse. More particles cross that way, so the net movement follows.

misconceptions.feedback: That would make the crowd even more crowded. More particles leave the crowded region than enter it.
Particles move constantly. It is the net movement that settles down, not the particles.

questions.prompt: Why does the total stay the same while solute moves?
hints: Think about where each particle goes.

acceptedIdeas: Solute only moves from place to place; none is made or lost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Diffusion moves solute between compartments but does not create or destroy it.

choices.label: Solute only moves from place to place; none is made or lost
Solute is replaced from outside the compartments
The two sides swap their solute exactly

questions.onCorrect: Diffusion only moves solute around. The total is conserved, so you can add the sides first.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing arrives from outside this closed system.
The sides don't swap. Net movement stops once the concentrations match.

questions.prompt: What word describes a membrane that lets a substance cross?
hints: The word starts with per-, meaning through.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A membrane is permeable to a substance if the substance can cross it.

questions.onCorrect: Permeable. Always check what a membrane is permeable to before predicting movement.

misconceptions.feedback: Impermeable means the opposite: nothing can cross.

citations.claim: Particles moving at random produce a net movement from the more crowded region to the less crowded one, which slows as the regions level out.
Random movement in both directions produces net movement from crowded to sparse and then equilibrium.
Diffusion is the net movement of a solute from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration.
With a permeable membrane, net solute movement runs from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side.
With equal fixed volumes and a freely crossing solute, equilibrium has equal amounts and the total is constant.
Equal volumes at equilibrium hold equal amounts of a freely crossing solute.
At equal concentration there is no net diffusion, though individual molecules still cross both ways.
Diffusion moves solute around and never destroys it, so the total is unchanged at equilibrium.
A membrane is selectively permeable: only some substances cross it, and a concentration difference cannot move a substance through a barrier that blocks it.
A concentration difference cannot move a substance through a barrier that blocks it.
24 units divide between two equal volumes, giving 12 each.
Diffusion produces a net flow down a concentration gradient.
The left side is more concentrated, so net solute movement is to the right.
The 16 units divide equally: 16 ÷ 2 = 8.
Nothing can cross, so each side keeps its starting amount: 12 on the left.
8 + 8 = 16 units. Diffusion does not destroy solute.
Equilibrium is dynamic: opposite flows balance on average.
Each side finishes with 8. The concentrated side loses 14 − 8 = 6.
The dye cannot cross, so its amounts do not change: 9 on the left.
Random movement in both directions produces net movement from crowded to sparse and then equilibrium.
